text: Randomised algorithms (随机化): randomness can make the expected running time good on every input, so no worst case can be prepared against you. Use mt19937 seeded with the clock, never rand() (small range on Windows) and never a fixed seed on Codeforces (hacks).

Typical uses: shuffle the input so an incremental algorithm runs in expected linear time; random priorities (treap, 第4章); random hash bases (第3章); trying random candidates when a large fraction of them work (e.g. "an element appearing in at least half the positions").

Minimum enclosing circle (P1742): three nested loops look like O(n³), but after a random shuffle the chance that point i lies outside the circle of the first i − 1 points is at most 3 / i, so the expected total is O(n). A sorted or adversarial order would really be cubic.

Constructive problems (构造) ask you to build an object (an array, a permutation, a graph) with given properties, or say it is impossible. There is no template; the usual path: solve tiny cases by hand or by brute force, guess a pattern, prove it (or at least check it by brute force for all small n), then code it.

Useful moves: start from an extreme (sorted, alternating, all equal); build in pairs or blocks; reduce n to n − 2 by fixing the ends; find an invariant (parity, sum mod k) that decides when it is impossible; and always write a checker for your own output.

Build a permutation of 1 … n whose neighbouring differences are all different. Zigzag between the ends: the differences are n − 1, n − 2, …, 1. The pattern was checked by Python for every n up to 39 before writing the program.
That habit, construct then verify with a brute-force checker on all small n, catches most wrong constructions before you submit.

In an interactive problem (交互题) your program talks to the judge: print a query, flush the output, read the reply, repeat, and answer within a query limit. Queries are the resource: binary search uses ⌈log₂ n⌉ of them; think about how many each strategy needs before coding.

Flush after every query: cout << x << endl; (endl flushes) or cout.flush() . This is the one place where endl is the right choice instead of "\n". Never print extra text, and stop immediately after the final answer.

Guess a number in 1 … 100 (hidden 37, then hidden 81). Here the judge's replies are prepared in the input, which is how you test an interactive program locally; on a real judge they arrive one by one.
For local testing, write a small judge program that knows the hidden value and answers each query, or feed prepared replies as above. Count queries in your own tests to check the limit.

Forgetting to flush is the classic "Idleness limit exceeded": your query sits in the buffer while the judge waits forever. Also, reading with ios::sync_with_stdio(false) is fine, but every query still needs a flush.
